Qualitative analysis with NVivo

From pages of text to a finding that a reader can check

Day one, 7 October 2026, 13:00 to 15:00

The method on paper, and what to do before day two

What qualitative data are, what thematic analysis is, what a code and a theme are, the six phases on a real review of published studies, where codes come from, and what a reader has to be able to check. You code three printed pages by hand and compare your labels with your neighbour. Before you leave you know how to get NVivo, how to choose a paper, and what to read.

Day two, 16 October 2026, 13:00 to 17:00

The same method, done in NVivo on a paper of your own

You create a project, import your paper, make codes with definitions, code passages, group the codes and write a memo. After the break I run four queries on a demonstration project and you run them on your paper, we read a word cloud, a word tree and a hierarchy chart, you export your codebook, and we go through the classwork screen by screen.

Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Windows & Mac. NVivo 15 for Windows help. Retrieved September 28, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/win/Content/projects-teamwork/work-with-projects-windows-mac.htm

Good afternoon. My name is Roxane de Waegh, and I am a Marie Skłodowska-Curie postdoctoral fellow here at the Islands and Small States Institute. My project, FAR-SIDS, studies foreign aid and remittances in small island developing states, and part of that project was a review of two hundred published studies that I coded by hand, which is the example I will use across these two days.

Over these two days you learn one method and one piece of software, and they are not the same thing. The method is thematic analysis, and it is what your dissertation and your classwork are assessed on. NVivo is a programme that keeps the record of that method for you. A person who knows the method and has no software can still produce an analysis that a reader can check, and a person who knows the software and not the method produces a project full of coloured labels that answers no question.

Look at the picture with me. On the left is what you start with, which is pages of text, and in your dissertation those pages will probably be interview transcripts or focus group notes. On the right is what you end with, which is a small number of themes and a claim about what they mean. Everything in these two days is about the middle, and about writing the middle down so that somebody else can follow it.

Today is on paper, and we do not open NVivo at all, which is deliberate. You will code three printed pages with a pen, you will compare what you wrote with the person sitting next to you, and you will not have written the same labels. Here is why that matters. Suppose one of you reads a Samoan villager saying that after the tsunami the family overseas sent money and without it the household could not have managed, and writes the label help from family. The person next to you reads the same sentence and writes obligation, because they know that in Samoa a son abroad is expected to send, and a house the whole village can see is where the money goes first. Both labels are defensible. The first one leads to a theme about coping after a disaster; the second leads to a theme about duty inside a family. Neither reader is wrong, and a dissertation that says which reading it took, and why, is a dissertation an examiner can trust. Producing that record is the whole of today.

Day two, 16 October, is practical from the first minute to the last, so you need your own laptop with NVivo installed and a paper of your own already chosen, and the last two slides today are about exactly that. NVivo runs on Mac and on Windows. I demonstrate on a Mac, because demonstrating on both would leave no time for anything else, and for everything we do in this module the two versions have the same tabs and the same windows, so you will be able to follow. The one habit to learn is that where I hold Control and click, Windows uses the right mouse button. The features that the Windows version has and the Mac does not, such as project maps and social network analysis, are outside this module (Lumivero, n.d.).

Day one · What these two days are for

Two days, one method, and a classwork you can finish at your desk on the second day

By 27 October you hand in a codebook and two query results from a paper of your choosing. What would you need to be able to do to produce them?

Day one

The method, on paper

What qualitative data are and what thematic analysis does with them. What a code and a theme are, the six phases of the method, and where codes come from, shown on a real review of published studies. Then twenty minutes with a pen on three printed pages, and what your labels look like next to your neighbour’s.

Day two

The same method, in NVivo

You create a project, import a paper of your own, make codes with definitions, code passages, group codes, write a memo and export a codebook. After the break, four queries and three charts, each with a line on what it cannot show. Nothing on day two is new method; every button does something named today.

The classwork

400 to 500 words, due 27 October

Your paper coded in NVivo to your own codes in two levels, each with a one sentence definition; the codebook exported; a word frequency query and a coding query run on the paper, with a screenshot of each; and two sentences on what the queries could not tell you. Every part is produced on a screen you will have used on 16 October.

Why this matters
The classwork is a small version of the qualitative chapter of a dissertation: a set of texts, a codebook a reader can open, and a claim you can defend from it.

Before I explain anything, look at the question on the slide. On 27 October you hand in a short piece of writing with a codebook and two screenshots attached, all made from one published paper you choose yourself. Tell me what you would need to be able to do to produce that. Somebody give me one skill.

The picture is the shape of the module. Today is the method, and we do it on paper, because a method you can do with a pen is a method you understand, and a button you press without understanding it produces a project full of coloured labels that answers no question. Between the days you get NVivo onto your laptop, choose one paper, and read two readings, and the last two slides today tell you exactly how. On 16 October we do the same work again in the software, on your paper, and we finish with queries that turn your coding into sentences you can put in a chapter.

Read the third card with me, because it is the assessment. Four hundred to five hundred words. Your paper coded to codes you made, in two levels, each with a one sentence definition. The codebook exported from NVivo. A word frequency query and a coding query, each with a screenshot. And two sentences on what the queries could not tell you, which is the part people leave out and the part that shows me you understood the method rather than the software. Every one of those five parts is made on a screen you will have used on 16 October, so if you are in the room on both days, the classwork is a matter of finishing what you started.

One more reason to care. Most of you will write a dissertation with interviews or focus groups in it, and the qualitative chapter of that dissertation is this classwork at a larger scale: a set of texts, a codebook a reader can open, and a claim you can defend by walking the reader from the claim back to a page. Everything today is about building that chain.

Day one · What we are analysing

Qualitative data are words, and a number cannot tell you why the money went where it went

Which of the two tells you how a household in Samoa got through the tsunami?

What the number can answer

How many, and how often

The 2021 Tongan household survey asked the same questions in every house and found that 90 in every hundred households had received cash from relatives outside the house in the previous twelve months (Tonga Statistics Department, 2022). It cannot say what any of that money was for, or what the family expected back.

What the sentence can answer

Why, in whose words, and what it meant

The villager tells you the money came when the household had lost everything, that the family overseas could be counted on, and that this was what carried them through. A sentence like this is qualitative data: a person’s account, in their own words, of what happened and what it meant (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 663).

Where you will meet it

Transcripts, notes, documents, published studies

Your dissertation will hold pages of words like the sentence: interview transcripts, focus group notes, policy documents or published papers. FAR-SIDS collects them too, in interviews and focus groups in Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros held before the household survey, so that the survey asks its questions in the households’ own words.

Why this matters
A number tells you how many; a sentence tells you why and what it meant. A dissertation needs both, and the sentence needs a method as much as the number does, which is what the rest of today is.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Tonga Statistics Department. (2022). Tonga 2021 household income and expenditure survey report. https://tongastats.gov.to/download/47/household-income-expenditure-survey/8078/tonga-2021-hies-report.pdf

Two pieces of evidence about the same subject, money sent home by relatives, and the question on the slide: which of the two tells you how a household in Samoa got through the tsunami? Take a moment and give me an answer.

The number on the left comes from a household survey. In 2021 the Tongan statistics office visited a sample of households, asked every one of them the same questions, and found that 90 in every hundred had received cash from relatives outside the house in the previous twelve months (Tonga Statistics Department, 2022). That is a strong and useful number, and it answers one kind of question: how many, and how often. It cannot tell you what the money was for, who decided, or what the family expected in return, because the survey never asked, and could not have asked in a form that fits in a box.

The sentence on the right comes from a study of rural Samoa after the tsunami of 2009, and it is one villager speaking: after the tsunami we lost everything, but we could count on our family overseas, and without remittances it would have been very hard (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 663). Read it again. It tells you the timing, that the money came when there was nothing left; it tells you the relationship, that the family overseas could be counted on; and it tells you the weight, that without the money it would have been very hard. That is qualitative data: a person’s own account of what happened and what it meant, in their own words.

So the answer to my question is the sentence, and the honest answer is both, because the number tells you the sentence is not one family’s story, and the sentence tells you what the number was for. Your dissertation will hold pages of the second kind: interview transcripts, focus group notes, documents, or published papers, which is what you will use for the classwork. My own project collects them too. In Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros we hold interviews and focus groups before the household survey, so that the survey asks about the obligations households actually name, in the words they use, rather than the words I arrived with.

Here is the difficulty that the rest of today is about. A survey comes with a method for turning answers into a number, and everybody accepts the number because they can see how it was made. Pages of words need a method too, or the reader is trusting your memory of what twelve people said. Thematic analysis is that method, and the next slide says what it is.

Day one · The method, named

Thematic analysis finds the patterns of meaning that run across a set of texts, and reports them as themes

If you read twelve interviews and write a paragraph about what each person said, have you analysed them?

What it is

A method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns

Braun and Clarke (2006, p. 79) define thematic analysis as “a method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns (themes) within data”. It works on interviews, focus groups, documents or published studies, and it is not tied to one theory, which is why it suits a dissertation (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 78 to 79).

What it is not

Not a summary, not a word count, not your questions with the answers under them

A paragraph on each interview describes; it does not find what runs across them. Counting words finds words, not meanings. Sorting answers by interview question is sorting, not analysis (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 94 to 95). And themes do not “emerge” on their own: you identify them, and saying so is part of the method (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 80).

Where FAR-SIDS uses it

On 1,133 abstracts, and soon on interviews

The FAR-SIDS review labelled the topics in 1,133 abstracts by hand and grouped the labels into 43 sub-themes and 10 groups (de Waegh, 2026). The fieldwork interviews and focus groups in Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros will be analysed the same way, and the review is the worked example for the rest of today.

Why this matters
Thematic analysis is what your classwork is assessed on, and what a qualitative dissertation chapter is expected to name and follow, phase by phase, where a reader can see it.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS systematic review: the search record, 14 September 2026 [Unpublished project record]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS all labels, 10 July 2026 and Label to theme mapping, 11 July 2026 [Unpublished project data files]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The question on the slide first. You have read twelve interviews and written a careful paragraph about what each person said. Have you analysed them? Hands up for yes.

You have described them, and description is where analysis starts, and it is not analysis. Look at the picture. Four transcripts, and in three of them the same meaning appears, a family overseas that can be counted on, and in three of them a second meaning, aid that arrives late while money from kin arrives first. A paragraph on each transcript would mention each of those once, in four different places, and the reader would never see that they are the same. Thematic analysis is the method that finds what runs across the set and names it, and the name it gives is a theme.

The definition on the left card is the one to write down, because you will cite it. Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke, in a paper published in 2006 that is your first reading, define thematic analysis as a method for identifying, analysing and reporting patterns, which they call themes, within data (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 79). Two features make it the right method for most dissertations. It works on any set of texts: interviews, focus groups, documents, or the published papers you will use for the classwork. And it is not tied to one theory, unlike grounded theory, which is built to produce a theory, or discourse analysis, which studies how language does its work; thematic analysis can be used inside either of those, or on its own (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 78 to 79).

The middle card is as important as the left one, because these are the ways a qualitative chapter goes wrong. A paragraph per interview is a summary. A count of words, which we will do on the second day, finds words and not meanings, and you will see on 16 October how the word support turns out to carry five different meanings in four papers. And putting your interview questions as headings with the answers under each is sorting, not analysis; Braun and Clarke list it among the ways a thematic analysis fails (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 94 to 95). One more habit to lose before you write a word: do not write that themes emerged from your data. They did not. You identified them, by a series of decisions, and Braun and Clarke call the emerging story a passive account that hides the researcher who did the work (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 80).

The right card is my own project, and it is the example for the rest of today. In June this year the review screened 1,133 abstracts of published studies on aid and remittances in small island states. As each abstract was read it was labelled by hand with the topics it discussed, and the labels were then grouped into 43 sub-themes and 10 groups (de Waegh, 2026). Those abstracts were the texts, exactly as your interviews will be, and the labels and groups are what the next slides take apart. The interviews and focus groups we hold in Jamaica, Tonga and the Comoros will be analysed the same way, in NVivo, which is the second day.

Day one · Three words to keep apart

Passage, code, theme: the three levels every slide today is about

An examiner doubts one of your themes. Which of the three do you show them first?

PassageA piece of the text itself: a sentence or a paragraph from a transcript or a paper, with the page or line it came from. The example is from the Samoa study we read this afternoon. Passages are the evidence; nothing above them is.
CodeA short label attached to a passage, with one sentence saying what belongs under it and what does not. The example is a code from the demonstration project we use on 16 October, and it holds the passage on the left (de Waegh, 2026). One passage can carry more than one code.
ThemeA group of codes with a name and a definition that make a claim about the data in relation to the research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). The example holds three codes: kinship, reciprocity and custom; church, religion and spirituality; gender and social relations.
The review, in the same three levels1,133 abstracts were the text. 758 labels were attached to them, and after cleaning 743 were grouped into 43 sub-themes and then into 10 groups (de Waegh, 2026). Your numbers will be smaller; the levels will be the same.
Why this matters
Keep the three words apart: a passage is text, a code is a label with a definition, a theme is a claim built from codes. Everything that goes wrong in a qualitative chapter is one of the three doing another one’s job.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS all labels, 10 July 2026 and Label to theme mapping, 11 July 2026 [Unpublished project data files]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Three words, and I want you to keep them apart for the rest of the two days, because most of what goes wrong in a qualitative chapter is one of the three doing another one’s job. The question first: an examiner doubts one of your themes. Which of the three levels do you show them first? Talk to your neighbour.

Read the picture from left to right. On the left is a passage, which is a piece of the text itself. This one is a sentence from the Samoa study you will read this afternoon: at the centre of this mechanism are the notions of service and obligation, tautua, from migrants toward the family, and it is on page 664 (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). A passage always comes with its page or its line, because it is the evidence, and nothing above it is evidence.

In the middle is a code. A code is a short label you attach to a passage, and it comes with one sentence saying what belongs under it and what does not. This one is called Kinship, reciprocity and custom, and its sentence says passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back. It is a real code from the project I use on 16 October, and the passage on the left sits under it (de Waegh, 2026). One passage can carry more than one code, and we come back to that.

On the right is a theme. A theme is a group of codes with a name and a definition, and the name makes a claim about the data in relation to your research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). This one is Culture, society and agency, and it holds three codes: the kinship code in the middle, a code on church and religion, and a code on gender and social relations. The examiner who doubts the theme opens it, finds the three codes, opens the kinship code, finds the passage, and reads page 664. That is the answer to my question: you show them the chain, and you start at the bottom, with the page.

The lower right box is the same three levels in my review, with the numbers. The text was 1,133 abstracts. The labels were 758, and after I cleaned the list 743 of them were grouped into 43 sub-themes and then into 10 groups (de Waegh, 2026). Your own dissertation will have twelve transcripts, perhaps sixty codes and four or five themes, and the levels are exactly the same. The next five slides take each level in turn: what a code is, why coding happens twice, what a theme is, the six phases that get you from the text to the themes, and where your codes come from.

Day one · The basic unit

A code is a short label attached to a passage, with one sentence saying what belongs under it

If I gave the same page to two of you, should you produce the same labels?

A code, written properly

Kinship, reciprocity and custom

Passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back.
The name says what the code is about, and the sentence says what you will and will not put under it. Anyone can apply this code to a new page and reach roughly the same answer you would.

The same code, written badly

Culture

No definition given.
This is a word and not a code. Six months from now you will not remember what you meant by it, and neither you nor your examiner can tell whether a given passage belongs under it. A code like this collects everything that fits nowhere else.

PassageThe piece of text you attach the label to. It can be a phrase, a sentence or a paragraph. The test is whether it still makes sense when you read it later on its own, away from the page it came from.
ReferenceThe word NVivo uses for one passage attached to one code. A code with twelve references has been applied to twelve pieces of text. You will see this word on the screen all afternoon on 16 October.
Why this matters
Writing the sentence takes about fifteen seconds at the moment you make the code; reconstructing it eight months later, from memory, across two hundred passages, is a job that rarely gets finished.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

The question first. If I gave the same page to two of you, should you produce the same labels? Turn to the person next to you and decide on an answer between you, and I will take two answers in a minute.

The answer is no, and that is not a failure. Two careful readers bring different backgrounds to the same page and see different passages in it, so what we ask for instead is that each of you can say what your labels mean, so that a third person can tell what you were doing. That is what the sentence under the code name is for, and it is the difference between the two cards on the slide.

Look at the left card with me. The name is Kinship, reciprocity and custom, and the sentence says passages on family obligation, customary giving, and what is owed back. If I hand you a new page now, you can apply that code and I can check your work. Now look at the right card. The name is Culture, and there is no sentence, so you cannot check anything, and in six months neither can the person who wrote it.

Here is what happens with a code like Culture. It becomes the place where every passage goes that does not obviously belong anywhere else, and by the end it has ninety references and means nothing. If you find a code in your own project growing much faster than the others, open it and read it, because it is probably doing this.

Two words in the lower boxes will follow us into the software. A passage is the piece of text you label, and there is no rule about how long it should be, because my test is whether it still makes sense on its own when you read it two months later, out of context. A reference is the word NVivo uses for one passage attached to one code, and you will see that word on your screen all afternoon on 16 October.

Day one · First cycle and second cycle

Coding happens twice: once to label the passages, and again to group the labels

Why not write down the four themes you expect to find and put the passages straight into them?

First cycle codingThe first pass over the material, where you attach a short label to each passage. Saldaña (2021) calls this first cycle coding. Nothing is grouped yet, and a label that turns out to be useless costs one line in a list.
Second cycle codingThe second pass, where you work on the labels themselves and decide which of them belong together and what the group is called. Saldaña (2021) calls this second cycle coding, and Charmaz (2006) calls the same move focused coding. In NVivo you do it by dragging codes onto each other.
The review these numbers come fromThe FAR-SIDS review asked what published research establishes about how foreign aid and money sent home by relatives support livelihoods in small island states. It read 1,133 abstracts and kept 201 studies (de Waegh, 2026). In the first pass each abstract got a short label for every topic it discussed, the way you will label a margin this afternoon, and that gave 758 labels. In the second pass the labels were read as a list, cleaned, and grouped: 743 labels into 43 sub-themes, and the 43 into 10 groups.
Clean the list before you group itThe list held Altriusm, Kindship and Marshal Islands, and one label split at a comma inside a bracket. Forty labels could not be used as they stood and twenty five came back corrected, which is how 758 became 743. Fix the spellings before you group, because a misspelt label splits one idea into two and your counts are wrong from then on (de Waegh, 2026).
Why this matters
Grouping a list of 743 short labels is an afternoon you can finish; rereading 201 studies to find your themes is not.
Sources

Saldaña, J. (2021). The coding manual for qualitative researchers (4th ed.). SAGE. https://www.sagepub.com/shop/buy-a-book/the-coding-manual-for-qualitative-researchers-4-273583

Charmaz, K. (2006). Constructing grounded theory: A practical guide through qualitative analysis. SAGE. https://uk.sagepub.com/en-gb/eur/constructing-grounded-theory/book255601

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS systematic review: the search record, 14 September 2026 [Unpublished project record]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS all labels, 10 July 2026 and Label to theme mapping, 11 July 2026 [Unpublished project data files]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The question on the slide wants an honest answer rather than a correct one. Why not write down the four themes you already expect to find, and drop the passages straight into them? It would be much faster, so tell me why we do not do that.

The usual result is that you find what you went looking for. If you fix the themes before you read, you notice every passage that fits one of them and you walk past everything else, and what you were not expecting is often what is worth writing about. I will show you one of those on 16 October, in a code I had to add while reading because nothing in my existing list would hold it.

So coding happens twice, and the two passes are different kinds of work. In the first pass you look at text and attach short labels. In the second pass you do not look at the text at all, because you are looking at your own list of labels and asking which of them say the same thing. Johnny Saldaña calls these first cycle and second cycle coding (Saldaña, 2021), and Kathy Charmaz calls the second one focused coding (Charmaz, 2006), which are different names for the same move.

The picture is the review that I use as the example across both days, and the lower left box says what it was. It asked what published research establishes about how foreign aid and money sent home by relatives support livelihoods in small island states. Four databases were searched on one day in June 2026, 1,133 records were screened by title and abstract, and 201 studies ended up in the review (de Waegh, 2026). Now follow the two passes on the review. In the first pass I read each abstract and wrote a short label for every topic it discussed, which is exactly what you will do in the margin of a printed page this afternoon, and across all the abstracts that gave 758 labels. In the second pass I stopped reading abstracts and read my own list of labels instead, asking which of them said the same thing, and the labels that said the same thing went under one name. That produced 43 sub-themes, and the same move again on the sub-themes produced 10 groups. So the direction of travel is from the text to a long list of labels, and from the long list to a short one, and the arithmetic works out at about seventeen labels for every sub-theme and four sub-themes for every group. Your own numbers will be smaller and the ratios will be similar.

The lower right box is what the list looked like before I could group anything. I had to read my own list, and it held Altriusm with the i and the u the wrong way round, Kindship with a d in it, Marshal Islands with one l, and one label that had been cut in half at a comma inside a bracket when the screening tool exported it. Forty of the 758 labels could not be used as they stood, and twenty five of those came back once they were respelt or joined together, which is how 758 became the 743 that went into the sub-themes (de Waegh, 2026). You will produce a list exactly like it, and the first time you see it you will think you have done something wrong, when in fact the work looks like this. So two habits: before you group, read your list and fix the spellings, because a misspelt label splits one idea into two and your counts are wrong from then on; and when you export labels from any tool, look at what happened to commas and brackets. And when you write your methods chapter, say what you cleaned, because a reader who sees you handling your own errors believes the rest of what you say.

One practical instruction for the first cycle. Be generous, because a useless label costs you one line in a list and you delete it in ten seconds, while a passage you never labelled is a passage you will never find again, since you will not reread the transcript.

Day one · From codes to a theme

A theme is a group of codes with a name and a definition, and a reader follows it back to the passages

Is “Money” a theme?

A theme, written properlyCulture, society and agency: everything the studies say about obligation, belief and the relationships money moves along. Three codes sit under it, each with its own sentence, and each code opens onto the passages with their page numbers. That chain is what a reader checks.
A topic is not yet a themeA theme called Money is a topic. A theme called What the money is expected to pay for, and who expects it, makes a claim that a reader can argue with. Braun and Clarke (2006, p. 82) define a theme as something important about the data in relation to the research question, not the most frequent thing in it.
Why this matters
The theme is only as strong as the chain under it: if the reader cannot get from the theme’s name to a page number in three steps, the theme rests on your word rather than on the record.

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The question on the slide: is Money a theme? Hands up for yes. It is a topic, and the difference matters for your dissertation, so look at the picture with me.

At the top is a theme from the demonstration project I use on day two, Culture, society and agency, and its definition says everything the studies say about obligation, belief and the relationships money moves along. Under it are three codes, each with its own one sentence definition: kinship, reciprocity and custom; church, religion and spirituality; and gender and social relations. Under the first code is a passage from the Samoa study you will read later this afternoon, with its page number: at the center of this mechanism are the notions of service and obligation, tautua, from migrants toward the family (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). That is the whole chain, theme, code, passage, page, and a reader who doubts the theme walks down the chain and reads the page.

Now the second passage in the picture. On the same page the authors say that a significant proportion of remittances goes to church donations, about 12 % (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). That sits under Church, religion and spirituality, and the count under that code says one source and two passages, because the next page of the same study gives church donations 9 % of remittances after the tsunami (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 665). I am showing you the counts on purpose. When I first coded this project the Church code was empty, and I was tempted to write that four studies about family money never mention the church. This page is the reason I went back to the text before writing that, and on day two I will ask you to do the same whenever a code of yours is empty.

So what makes a theme rather than a topic? Braun and Clarke say a theme captures something important about the data in relation to your research question (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 82). Frequency helps but does not decide it. Money is a topic because it makes no claim, and my review had the same problem in a different form: the most common label of all was Remittance, on 110 of the abstracts, and it is a topic, because every study in a review about remittances is about remittances (de Waegh, 2026). The theme is what the studies say remittances do. What the money is expected to pay for, and who expects it, is a theme, because it says something a reader can disagree with, and because you can put codes and passages under it that support or weaken the claim.

Day one · The method

Thematic analysis runs through six phases, and the fourth is the one that catches your mistakes

Which of these six phases do you think takes the longest, and which one do you think is most often skipped?

The six phases of Braun and Clarke (2006, pp. 87 to 93), in the order the work happens.

What the review did at each phaseIt read and labelled the 1,133 records in one pass, so phases one and two ran together, which is a shortcut you do not need with twelve interviews. It grouped 743 labels into 43 sub-themes and 10 groups (phase three), opened each group and moved passages that did not belong (phase four), named the groups (phase five), and the written report, phase six, is the paper being written this autumn.
Phase four, in plain wordsYou open a theme, you read every passage under it one after another, and you ask of each one whether it belongs there. After phase three you have a tidy list on a page and it looks finished, and it usually is not. In NVivo this phase is one double click.
Why this matters
Opening a theme and reading the twenty passages inside it costs an afternoon; finding out at the viva that eight of them were about something else can cost a resubmission.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

de Waegh, R. (2026). FAR-SIDS all labels, 10 July 2026 and Label to theme mapping, 11 July 2026 [Unpublished project data files]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

These six phases come from a paper by Virginia Braun and Victoria Clarke published in 2006, which is one of the two readings you do before 16 October, and the phases are on pages 87 to 93 of that paper (Braun and Clarke, 2006). Read them across the picture with me, and then the question: which of these six takes the longest, and which one do you think is most often skipped?

The longest is the second, the labelling, and nobody is surprised by that. The one most often skipped, in my experience of the review and in what supervisors say about dissertations, is the fourth, and I would like you to remember that answer.

Phase one is reading everything once without labelling, and phase two is attaching the labels. In the review those two ran together, because I could not read 1,133 abstracts twice, so I labelled as I screened. You do not need that shortcut with twelve interviews, and the method is better without it, because a label you attach on a first reading is a label you attach before you know what the whole set contains. Phase three is grouping the labels, and in the review the 743 labels went into 43 sub-themes and then into 10 groups.

Phase four is the one that is easy to skip, so let me be specific about what it is. You open a theme, you read every passage under it one after another, and you ask of each one whether it belongs there. Why does this get skipped? After phase three you have a tidy list on a page and it looks as if you have finished. When I opened my own sub-themes in July, more than one of them held passages that belonged somewhere else, and the tidy list had hidden that. In NVivo phase four is a double click, and that is one of the strongest reasons to use the software at all.

Phase five is naming, which is the theme slide from earlier: a theme called Money is a topic, while a theme that makes a claim can be argued with. Phase six is the write up, and Braun and Clarke are clear that writing is part of the analysis and not a report on it, because you find out what you think while you write (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 87 to 93). For the review, phase six is the paper I am writing this autumn, so the review has been through five and is in the sixth.

Day one · Two ways in

Your codes come from the text as you read, or from a list you wrote first, and your methods chapter says which

You have read three interviews and a theory paper. Which of the two are you actually doing?

From the text

You read, and you write a label for what is in front of you

Braun and Clarke (2006, pp. 83 to 84) call this inductive coding. You do not know the list in advance. It suits a question nobody has answered in that setting before, and it takes longer, because the list only settles once most of the material has been read.

From a list made first

You decide the codes in advance and apply them

Braun and Clarke (2006, pp. 83 to 84) call this deductive, or theoretical, coding. The list usually comes from a framework or from earlier studies. It is faster and it can be tested, and it cannot show you anything your framework has no word for.

Both, which is the usual choice

You start from a list and add codes when the text asks for them

This is what the demonstration project does and what your dissertation will probably do. It is a legitimate choice, and it stops being legitimate when you do not say so, because a reader then cannot tell which of your themes were found and which were assumed.

Why this matters
One sentence in your methods chapter names the route, and if you took both it says where the starting list came from and which codes you added while reading.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Earlier I said not to go straight to your four themes. That is not the same as saying you may not start with a list of codes, and the difference is on this slide. There are two ways your codes can arrive, and I want you to be able to name which one you are using, because your examiner will ask. The first way is that you read the text and write a label for what you find, which Braun and Clarke call inductive coding, and you do not know your list in advance. The second way is that you decide your codes before you read, usually from a framework or from earlier studies, and then apply them, which they call deductive or theoretical coding (Braun and Clarke, 2006, pp. 83 to 84).

Now the question on the slide. You have read three interviews and a theory paper, so which of the two are you actually doing? Talk to your neighbour for thirty seconds and then tell me.

The honest answer for nearly everybody in this room is both. You come in carrying a framework, because you have just spent a semester reading, and then the interviews say something the framework has no word for and you make a new code. That is the third card, and it is what I did in the demonstration project. What is not acceptable is failing to say so, because a reader then has no way to tell which of your themes you found and which you brought with you.

So here is the practical instruction, and it is one sentence in your methods chapter. Say which route you took, and if you took both, say where the starting list came from and name the codes you added while reading. On 16 October I will show you where NVivo keeps that record for you, in a memo, so that you are not trying to remember it in April.

There is a second choice of the same kind, and one sentence on it is enough for today. You can code what a passage says on its surface, which Braun and Clarke call semantic coding, or you can code the assumption underneath it, which they call latent coding: the villager who says the family overseas could be counted on is, on the surface, describing help, and underneath, describing an obligation (Braun and Clarke, 2006, p. 84). Most dissertations code at the surface and interpret afterwards, and your methods chapter says which you did.

Day one · The standard the activity practises

A reader can check a qualitative finding when every step from the pages to the themes is written down

When you write in your dissertation that you identified a theme in your data, what are you asking the examiner to take on trust?

One

What you read

Which transcripts, documents or articles you worked from, how many there were, and how you chose them. If you interviewed twelve people, a reader has to see all twelve, so that they can judge whether a theme runs across the twelve interviews or comes from the three you liked best.

Two

What you labelled, and what each label means

Every code you made, the one sentence definition that says what belongs under it, and the passages under each one. This document is the codebook, and an examiner may very well ask for it.

Three

How the labels became themes, and who decided

Which labels you grouped together, what you called the group, what you dropped, and on whose judgement. Braun and Clarke (2019) treat the researcher’s own judgement as a resource for the analysis, so naming the person who decided is part of the method.

Why this matters
These three records are what turn a chapter of quotations into a finding, and they are the part of the work a supervisor can still help you repair after the fieldwork is over, so you build them while you code.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101. https://doi.org/10.1191/1478088706qp063oa

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597. https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676X.2019.1628806

I want to start with the question on the slide, and I would like an answer from the room before I give you mine. When you write in your dissertation that you identified a theme in your data, what are you asking the person marking it to take on trust? Take a moment, and somebody give me one thing.

My own answer has three parts, and they are the three boxes in the picture. The first is the set of material you read, because if I cannot see which interviews you worked from and how many there were, I cannot tell whether your theme came from all of them or from the two that were most interesting. The second is the labels you attached and what each label means, because a label with no definition is only a word, and a word can be stretched to cover anything, which is what happens when a student is short of evidence. The third is how those labels turned into themes, and who made that decision.

That third one makes some people uncomfortable, so let me say it plainly. In this method there is no rule that converts labels into themes on its own, and you are the one who decides. Braun and Clarke, whose 2006 paper is your first reading, wrote a second paper in 2019 in which they treat the researcher’s judgement as a resource for the analysis rather than a bias to be removed (Braun and Clarke, 2019). So you do not hide the judgement, you write it down, which is what a memo does, and we will write one together on day two.

Think about your own dissertation for a moment. At some point somebody will read your findings chapter and decide whether to believe you, and these three records are what they will use to decide. They are also the part of the work that is hardest to repair afterwards, because if you finish your fieldwork with no codebook and no record of your decisions, no supervisor can reconstruct them for you.

In twenty minutes you will code three pages with a pen, and I will ask you for exactly these three records: what you read, which is the three pages; what you labelled and what each label means; and, when you compare with your neighbour, who decided what and why.

Day one · Activity, on paper

Code three printed pages by hand, then compare your labels with the person next to you

Before you read: what would you expect a household in Samoa to do when aid after a disaster is slow to arrive?

What you have in front of youPages 663 to 665 of Le Dé and colleagues (2015), printed. The study is about rural Samoa after the tsunami of 2009 and cyclone Evan in 2012, and these three pages carry the main finding, a participant’s own words, and an explanation from other authors that competes with it. You need a pen and the margin, and nothing else.
Le Dé and colleagues (2015), the full article
What to do, in order
  1. Read all three pages once without writing anything. This is phase one, and it takes about four minutes.
  2. Read them again. Every time a passage says something about how households got through the disaster, underline it and write a short label in the margin next to it, of no more than six words.
  3. Next to three of your labels, write one sentence saying what would and would not belong under it.
  4. Count your labels and write the number at the top of the first page.
  5. Swap pages with the person next to you and read their labels against your own.
Why this matters
This is the whole of first cycle coding, done with a pen in twenty minutes, and everything NVivo does on 16 October is this, kept in a form you can search and count.
Sources

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Put your laptops away for this, because you need a pen and paper only. Before you read anything, answer the question at the top of the slide out loud: what would you expect a household in Samoa to do when aid after a disaster is slow to arrive? I want you to have committed to an expectation before you read, so that you notice when the paper disagrees with you.

You have three pages in front of you, pages 663 to 665 of a study by Loïc Le Dé and colleagues about rural Samoa after the tsunami of 2009 and cyclone Evan in 2012 (Le Dé et al., 2015). I chose these three pages because they carry the main finding, they carry one participant speaking in their own words, and they carry another group of authors explaining the same pattern in a completely different way, which is a lot for three pages.

Read the five steps with me. Read all three pages once without writing anything, which takes about four minutes. Then read them again, and this time, every time a passage says something about how households got through the disaster, underline it and write a short label next to it, with no more than six words in the label, and write it down rather than keeping it in your head, because in ten minutes you will not remember it.

Step three is the one people want to skip. Next to three of your labels, write one sentence saying what would and would not belong under that label. I am asking for only three because it is slow, and I want you to feel how slow, because the slowness is the lesson of the exercise.

Then count your labels, write the number at the top, and swap pages with the person next to you. You have twenty minutes and I will walk round. If you are stuck on what counts as a passage worth labelling, ask me rather than sitting there, because the answer is usually that you are being too careful.

Day one · What just happened

Two careful readers label the same page differently, and what you do about that is part of the method

Who has a label that their neighbour does not have at all? Read it out.

You will have found this

Different numbers of labels

Some of you wrote six labels and some wrote twenty, and neither is wrong yet. A reader can work with six and can work with twenty, as long as each one has a definition and the passages under it match it.

And this

The same passage under different names

The sentence about families overseas helping when aid was slow will have been labelled several different ways in this room. Those labels are candidates for the same group, and finding that out is second cycle coding.

And, most usefully, this

A label that only one of you wrote

Somebody in this room labelled the obligation the authors call tautua, the service owed to the family (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664), and somebody else read straight past it. That passage is where one reader brought something to the page that another reader did not.

What to do with disagreementYou do not average it. You talk it through, you decide, and you write the decision down. Braun and Clarke (2019) argue that agreement between coders is not what makes reflexive thematic analysis credible, and that the record of the decisions is. If you do use a second coder, report what you disagreed on and not only the share you agreed on.
What this becomes on 16 OctoberThe labels you have just written in a margin are codes. The sentences you wrote next to three of them are the definitions. The disagreement you have just had with your neighbour is what a memo records. On 16 October you do all three of those in NVivo, on a paper of your own choosing.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597. https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676X.2019.1628806

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Hands up who wrote more than fifteen labels. Hands up who wrote fewer than eight. Now the question on the slide: who has a label that their neighbour does not have at all? Read it out to the room.

The first card is that you wrote different numbers of labels, and that is not yet a problem, because a reader can follow six labels and can follow twenty, as long as each has a definition and the passages under it match. The second is that the same passage got different names from different people, and the sentence about families overseas helping when external aid was slow will have been labelled several ways in this room. Those different names are candidates to be grouped together, and noticing that is the second pass we talked about earlier.

The third is the one I care about most. Somewhere in the room, one person labelled the obligation that the authors call tautua, the service a migrant owes their family, and the person next to them read straight past it (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 664). Who labelled it, and what did you call it? That difference is not noise. It is a reader bringing something to the page that another reader did not bring, and it is why Braun and Clarke treat the researcher’s judgement as part of the method.

So what do you do about disagreement? You do not average it, and you do not go looking for a number that says you agreed 80% of the time, because for this method that number does not mean what people think it means, which Braun and Clarke (2019) say directly in the second paper on your reading list. You talk it through, you decide, and you write the decision down. On 16 October I will show you where NVivo keeps that written decision, and the first memo we write together will be exactly this kind of disagreement.

Everything you have just done with a pen has a name in the software. Your margin labels are codes, your three sentences are definitions, and your argument with your neighbour is a memo, which covers the whole of the first half of 16 October.

Before 16 October you request NVivo and you choose a paper, and both are on this slide. The first question: how long do you think a software request takes to be approved here? I do not know the answer for your account, and that is why I am asking you to do it this week rather than the day before, because the request goes to a person, and people have queues.

Here is what you are asking for. NVivo 15 is made by a company called Lumivero, it is free to you under the University site licence, and it runs on both Mac and Windows. Everything you will see on my screen on 16 October is NVivo 15 on a Mac, and where a menu differs on Windows I say both out loud; the Windows help pages are linked here and cover every step we do. Tell me now if you are on Windows so that I know how many of you there are.

Follow the five steps on the left with me. The first link is the University IT Services page for NVivo, and it will ask you to sign in with your UM IT Account before it shows you anything, so have that to hand. Follow the request on that page, download the installer for your own machine, and then, because this is the step most often skipped, open NVivo once before 16 October and check that it actually starts. Step five matters as much as the other four. If that page has moved, or the request does not go through, or the programme will not open, email me this week, because I can sort out a licence problem in the first week of October and I cannot sort one out at one o’clock on 16 October with twenty of you in the room.

Now the second question: why would it matter whether you can select the text of your PDF with your mouse? There are two kinds of PDF. One kind holds real text, so when you drag your mouse across a sentence the sentence highlights and you can copy it. The other kind is a photograph of a page, usually from a scanner, and dragging your mouse across it selects nothing, because as far as the computer is concerned there are no words there, only a picture. You can still code the second kind, because NVivo lets you draw a box around a region and attach a code to it, but you cannot run any of the queries we do on the second afternoon, since a word frequency query counts words and a picture contains no words, and the classwork asks you for that query.

So the check on the right takes two minutes. Download the PDF, open it, drag your mouse across one sentence, copy it, and paste it into an email to yourself. If words appear, you are fine, and if nothing appears, choose a different paper, because there are plenty of papers. Pick something on a small island or small state topic that you actually want to read, because you are going to read it closely twice and then write four hundred words about it. Twenty pages or so is a good size. Email me the file name by 12 October so that I know what everyone is working on and can spot a problem before you arrive.

Day two · Demonstration 1 of 17

Creating the project: one file on your own disk, made before you have anything to put in it

Where on your laptop are you going to keep this file, and where is the second copy going to live?

The New Project window in NVivo 15 on a Mac, with the fields the steps name
The clicks, in order
  1. Open NVivo. On the opening screen choose Create New Project, or from the menu bar choose File then New Project.
  2. In Save As, type a name you will recognise in April. ISS5220 my project is better than Untitled.
  3. In Where, choose a folder you can find again, and not Downloads.
  4. Write one sentence in Description. Leave Text Content Language at English unless your paper is in another language; it sets which common words the word frequency query ignores this afternoon.
  5. Click Create Project. The window you get is empty, and that is correct.
What you should see

A single file ending in .nvpx in the folder you chose, and an empty NVivo window with nothing in Files and nothing in Codes. Everything you import goes inside that one file.

Why this matters
That one file is the whole project, so copy it somewhere else at the end of every session you work in it.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Create a new project. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/projects-teamwork/create-a-new-project.htm

Open NVivo with me, and if it is installed, follow every click, and if it is not, watch and see me at the break. I am building a new, empty project on my screen beside you, so what you see me click is what you click. The pictures on the slides are a different file: the demonstration project, which holds four studies from the review that I coded before today. I use its pictures because an empty project shows you almost nothing, while the finished one shows you where this afternoon ends. The question on the slide before we start is not rhetorical: where on your laptop are you going to keep this file, and where is the second copy going to live? Have an answer by the end of this slide, because I am going to ask you again.

On the opening screen there is a button that says Create New Project, and if you have gone past that screen you can always get there from the menu bar with File and then New Project, and you get the window on the screen (Lumivero, n.d.). Save As is the file name, so type something you will recognise in April, because Untitled will not help you then. Where is the folder, and I am asking you not to put it in Downloads, because Downloads is where files get lost. Write one sentence in the Description now, because it is the first thing a reader sees and it takes ten seconds.

Look properly at Text Content Language, because it comes back this afternoon. It sets which common words are ignored when NVivo counts word frequencies, words like the, and, and of, so leave it at English unless your paper is in another language.

Click Create Project. Your window is now empty, with nothing in Files and nothing in Codes, and that is exactly right, because you have not imported anything yet. Now look in your folder. There is one file, ending in dot n v p x, and that one file is the entire project, because everything goes inside it, including copies of the PDFs you import. That is convenient and it is also the whole risk, so, my question again: where is your second copy going to live? By five o’clock this file will hold one paper, somewhere around twenty codes and one memo, and you copy it to a drive or to cloud storage the moment you stop working.

Day two · Demonstration 2 of 17

The NVivo window: the navigation on the left, the list in the middle, the item on the right

Look at your own screen. Which of the three areas is the one you have not touched yet?

The demonstration project: navigation on the left, the list of files in the middle, and the Samoa study by Le Dé and colleagues (2015) open on the right
The clicks, in order
  1. The navigation, down the left, is a list of places, not of files or codes. Data holds your Files, Coding holds your Codes, Cases holds the sources you have classified, and Notes holds your memos. Clicking a place changes what the middle shows.
  2. The list, in the middle, shows whatever is in the place you clicked. If you clicked Codes, it is your list of codes.
  3. The item, on the right, is whatever you double clicked, a paper or a code with all its passages. This is where you read and where you code.
  4. The ribbon along the top has seven tabs. You need five today: Home for coding, Import to bring material in, Create for codes and memos, Explore for the queries after the break, and Share to export your codebook at the end.
What you should see

If a menu is greyed out, the wrong place is selected on the left. If Import will not let you import files, click Files on the left first. If a coding option is grey, you have not selected any text.

Why this matters
The three areas depend on each other, left to right, and knowing that solves most of what goes wrong this afternoon.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/welcome.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Look at the picture and then at your own window. The picture is the demonstration project, with four files in the list and one of them open; yours has an empty list, and the three areas sit in the same places. The question first: which of the three areas have you not touched yet? Most of you will say the one on the right, because you have created a project and imported nothing.

There are three areas and they work from left to right. On the far left is the navigation, and what matters is that it is a list of places and not a list of files or codes: Data holds your Files, Coding holds your Codes, and Cases and Notes we come to later. When you click one of these, the middle changes. The middle is the list of whatever is in the place you just clicked, so if you click Codes on the left the middle fills with your codes. The right is the item, whatever you double clicked, a paper or a code with every passage in it, and that is where you read and where you code (Lumivero, n.d.).

Now the habit that will save you twenty minutes this afternoon. When a menu is greyed out and you cannot understand why, it is almost always because the wrong place is selected on the left. If the Import menu will not let you import a file, click Files on the left first and then try again, and if the coding options are grey, you have not selected any text. Remember that and you will solve most of your own problems today.

Along the top there are seven tabs and you need five of them. Home is where the Code button lives, so you use it more than any other. Import brings material in, Create makes codes and memos, Explore runs the queries after the break, and Share gets your codebook out at the end. Ignore the other two today. One difference for those of you on Windows that comes up all afternoon: wherever I say hold Control and click, you click with the right mouse button, and the same menu appears.

Day two · Demonstration 3 of 17

Importing the paper copies it into the project file, so the original on your disk is never touched

If you delete the PDF from your Downloads folder tomorrow, what happens to your project?

The demonstration project after importing, with four studies from the review in the Files list
The clicks, in order
  1. On the left, under Data, click Files. Nothing in the Import menu works until you do.
  2. On the ribbon click Import, then Files, then PDFs... A PDF imported as a PDF keeps its layout, its page numbers and its figures.
  3. Find your paper and click Import. A long paper takes a few seconds.
  4. Your paper appears in the list. Double click it and it opens on the right.
  5. Above the open paper, check that Selection Mode is set to T, the letter, which selects text. The rectangle selects a region, which you need only for a PDF that has no real text in it.
What you should see

Your paper in the Files list, with Codes and References both at zero. The Codes and References columns in this list count differently from the codebook we export at the end, so the passage counts you report in your classwork come from the codebook and not from this list.

Why this matters
Because the project file holds a copy, deleting the original PDF does nothing to your project; it also means that if you import the wrong version of a paper, fixing the file on your disk changes nothing inside NVivo, and you have to import it again.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Documents and PDFs. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/files/documents-and-pdfs.htm

The question first, because it catches people out. If you delete the PDF from your Downloads folder tomorrow, what happens to your project? Hands up for nothing happens, and hands up for the project breaks.

Nothing happens. When you import, NVivo takes a copy and puts it inside the project file, which is why the file grows, and why you can move the project to another laptop and everything comes with it. It also means the reverse: if you import the wrong version of a paper and then fix the file on your disk, NVivo still has the old copy, and you have to import it again (Lumivero, n.d.).

Follow the clicks with me. On the left, under Data, click Files, and I said this on the last slide and I am saying it again, because if you do not click Files first, every option under Import is greyed out and you will think the programme is broken. Now Import on the ribbon, then Files, then PDFs. Notice that there is also Documents on that menu, which is for Word files and plain text; for a journal article, use PDFs, because it keeps the layout and the page numbers, and you will want the page numbers when you quote something.

Find your paper, click Import, and wait a moment. It appears in the list, and when you double click it, it opens on the right. One setting to check before you do anything else: above the open paper there is Selection Mode with two small buttons, a letter T and a rectangle. Make sure the T is chosen, because that selects text, while the rectangle selects a box, which you only need for a PDF that is a picture of a page.

Look at the two columns in the picture, Codes and References. Your paper shows zero in both. The demonstration project shows numbers because its four studies are already coded, and those two columns count differently from the codebook we export at the end of the afternoon, so the passage counts you report in your classwork come from the codebook and not from this list.

Some of you are finding the sentence much harder than the name, and that difficulty is what we did on paper on the first day.

Here are the clicks. Under Coding on the left, click Codes. On the ribbon, Create, then Code, then New Code, and you get the Code Properties window that is on the screen (Lumivero, n.d.). Two fields matter: Name, at the top, which should be no more than six words and should read as a label rather than as a sentence, and Description underneath, which is one sentence saying what belongs under this code and what does not.

Description is the field most people leave empty, and it is the one an examiner reads, because when you export your codebook at the end of today, the codebook is exactly these two fields side by side, and a codebook with empty descriptions is a list of words that a reader cannot check. Chapter 7 of Beekhuyzen and Bazeley, which you read for today, is about making codes like this one. Day two · Demonstration 5 of 17

Coding a passage to one code, and the same passage to a second code

Can one sentence belong under two codes at once, and if it can, is that a mistake?

A selected sentence in a PDF with the Code menu open. Every route to coding it is on this one menu.
The clicks, in order
  1. Select the text you want to code by dragging across it.
  2. On the Home tab click the arrow next to Code, or hold Control and click the selected text. Both give you the menu on the screen.
  3. Under Code Selection, choose To Existing Codes or Cases..., tick the code you want, and click Select.
  4. If the code does not exist yet, choose To New Code... instead and make it on the spot, with its description. This is inductive coding, at the moment you notice something.
  5. To code the same passage to a second code, select it again and repeat. Nothing is removed. When you are coding quickly, use Quick Code Selection... or the Recent Codes or Cases list at the bottom of the same menu.
What you should see

In the demonstration project one sentence of the Samoa study is coded to two codes, Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique and Remittance flows, motives and behaviour. It reads: remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653).

Why this matters
Coding one passage to two codes is not double counting; it records a passage that does two jobs, and it is what makes the coding query after the break possible.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Manual coding techniques. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/coding/coding-techniques.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

The question first: can one sentence belong under two codes at once, and if it can, is that a mistake? Talk to your neighbour for twenty seconds. It can, and it is not a mistake, and I would like you to hold that thought, because it is the reason one of the queries after the break works at all.

Now the clicks. Select the text by dragging across it, exactly as you would in any programme. Then either click the small arrow next to Code on the Home tab of the ribbon, or hold Control and click on the text you selected, and both give you the menu on the screen (Lumivero, n.d.). The top group says Code Selection, and the first option is To Existing Codes or Cases, which opens a list where you tick the code you want and click Select. That is coding.

The second option is To New Code, and notice that this has a name from the first day, because it is inductive coding: you are reading, you see something your list has no word for, and you make the code at that moment, with its description. Now the double coding. Select the same sentence again and code it to a second code, and nothing is removed, so the sentence now sits under both.

Here is a real example from the demonstration project. In the Samoa study there is a sentence that says remittances interact with external aid, since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653). That one sentence is about aid and about remittances at the same time, so I coded it to both, and I am coding it to both on my project now so that you see the two rounds of clicks. After the break I run a query that asks for every passage coded to both of those codes together, and that sentence is what comes back. It is about the question the whole review was asking, and the query can find it only because I coded the passage twice.

One more click before you start. When you are coding fast, going through that menu every time is slow, so use Quick Code Selection, which gives you a search box, or pick from Recent Codes or Cases at the bottom of the menu. Code ten passages in your own paper now, and I will come round.
