Everybody stop coding and do this with me. Under Coding on the left, click Codes, find your biggest code, the one with the most references, and double click it. Now the question: does everything in it belong together? Read the passages, and I will give you three minutes and ask for hands afterwards.

While you read, look at the two tabs. Summary tells you which files the code appears in and how much of each file it covers, and Reference gives you the passages themselves, grouped under the file they came from (Lumivero, n.d.). In the picture the demonstration project has Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique open. It holds three passages, two from the Samoa study and one from the study by Wood, Otor and Dornan about why aid projects are less effective in the Pacific, and it covers 0.19% of the Samoa paper. That last number deserves a comment: coverage is usually tiny, because you are coding sentences out of a twenty page article, and a small percentage does not mean you have done badly.

Hands up who found a passage in their biggest code that does not belong. Most of you, which is phase four working. To take it out, select the passage, and on the Home tab click Uncode and then From This Code.

On paper, checking a theme properly means finding twenty passages across nine transcripts and reading them one after another, and it takes an afternoon, which is why it so often does not happen. Here it is one double click. If there is a single reason to put your analysis in this software rather than in a notebook, it is this screen, and if you use NVivo all year and never once open your own codes and read them, you have paid the cost of learning it and taken little of the benefit.

What this screen will not do for you. It shows you that three passages are there, and it does not tell you whether they mean the same thing; only you reading them does that.

Day two · Demonstration 7 of 17

Coding stripes and highlighting: what you have coded on the page, and what you have walked past

Which part of your paper have you coded nothing from, and is that because there is nothing there?

The Samoa study with highlighting on and coding stripes down the right, each stripe labelled with its code
The clicks, in order
  1. Open a paper you have coded.
  2. Above the open paper, click Coding Stripes and choose All. Coloured bars appear down the right side, one for each code, labelled with its name.
  3. Click Highlight and choose Coding for Selected Items..., tick Codes, and click Select. Coded text turns yellow in the page itself.
  4. Scroll through the whole paper and look for the long stretches with no stripe next to them.
  5. Turn both off again when you want to read cleanly, by choosing None in each menu.
What you should see

In the picture the abstract of the Samoa study is highlighted sentence by sentence, and each stripe on the right carries the name of a code. If you choose Coding for All Codes or Cases instead, the whole page turns yellow, because a case covers the whole file; you meet cases after the break.

What this cannot tell you. Why a stretch of the paper has no stripe. A long gap is either a part of the paper with nothing for your question in it, or the point where you stopped reading properly, and only rereading tells you which.

Why this matters
Coding can drift: you start attentive and by page fourteen you may be skimming. The stripes show that in ten seconds, so run this check before you decide you have finished a paper.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Manual coding techniques. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/coding/coding-techniques.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Do this one with me on your own paper, because it is quick and it will tell you something you may not want to hear. Open a paper you have coded. Above it, click Coding Stripes and choose All, and coloured bars appear down the right hand side, one for each code, each one labelled. Then click Highlight and choose Coding for Selected Items, tick Codes in the window that opens, and click Select, and the coded text turns yellow in the page (Lumivero, n.d.).

Now scroll through the whole paper slowly and ask the question on the slide: which part have you coded nothing from, and is that because there is nothing there for your question, or because you started skimming at that page? Look at the picture, which is the Samoa study in the demonstration project. The abstract is covered in stripes and the middle of the paper has far fewer, and part of that is real, because the methods section is about how the authors ran their workshops, but part of it is me reading less carefully by page twelve. Coding drifts, and this screen shows you where in about ten seconds.

A point that confuses people. If you choose Coding for All Codes or Cases instead, the whole page goes yellow and one stripe runs the entire length of the paper. That is not a coding error, it is a case, which is attached to the whole source rather than to a passage, and you meet cases after the break. Until then, choose Selected Items and tick Codes.

Turn both off when you want to read normally, by choosing None in each menu. They are a check you run, not a view you work in.

Day two · Demonstration 8 of 17

Grouping codes under a parent code, which is second cycle coding in NVivo

Look at your list of codes. Which two of them say the same thing in different words?

The demonstration project’s codes: six parents, and seventeen children indented under them
The clicks, in order
  1. Read your own list of codes and decide which of them belong together. Do this on paper first if it helps, because it is thinking and not clicking.
  2. Make a new code for the group, named for what the group is about, with its own description: Create, then Code, then New Code.
  3. Click a code you want to move, wait a moment, then drag it onto the group code. It moves underneath and is now a child code.
  4. Repeat until every code is either inside a group or deliberately outside one.
  5. If you want the parent to show the passages of its children as well as its own, hold Control, click the parent, choose Get Info, and tick Aggregate coding from child codes.
What you should see

Six parents and seventeen children. Sixteen of the children came from the review’s own coding frame, and one, Remittances arrive before the aid does, was added while reading the Samoa study, because no code in the frame held what that study claims about timing. The memo on the next slide records why.

What this cannot tell you. Which codes belong together. The software moves whatever you drag, and the judgement that two labels say the same thing is yours.

Why this matters
This is the move from 743 labels to 43 sub-themes that you saw on the first day, and it is the same move whether you have twenty codes or seven hundred.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Create codes manually. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/nodes/create-theme-node-manually.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Beekhuyzen, J., & Bazeley, P. (2024). Qualitative data analysis with NVivo (4th ed.). SAGE. https://collegepublishing.sagepub.com/products/qualitative-data-analysis-with-nvivo-4-284044

Stop clicking for a minute and look at your own list of codes. The question on the slide: which two of them say the same thing in different words? Find them, because this is thinking and not clicking, and you may want to do it on paper.

What you are doing now is the second pass we talked about on the first day, the move from 743 labels to 43 sub-themes, and it is the same move with smaller numbers. On screen it works like this: make a new code for the group, named for what the group is about, with its own description, then click one of the codes you want to put inside it, wait a moment, and drag it onto the group code. It moves underneath and becomes what NVivo calls a child code, and you repeat until every code is either inside a group or deliberately outside one. Beekhuyzen and Bazeley cover parent and child codes in their coding chapters.

Look at the picture, which is the demonstration project’s list of codes. Six parents with seventeen children under them. Aid and donor politics has two children, Livelihoods and wellbeing has four, and your classwork asks you for at least two levels, so this is the shape you are aiming for. Sixteen of those children came from the coding frame of the review, and one of them, Remittances arrive before the aid does, I added while reading the Samoa study, because nothing in the frame held what that study claims about timing. I put it under Remittances and diaspora, because the passages are about remittances, and on the next slide you will see the note I wrote about why it did not go into Aid effectiveness.

One setting to know about, because it will confuse you otherwise. Hold Control, click a parent code, choose Get Info, and there is a box called Aggregate coding from child codes. With it off, the parent shows only passages coded directly to the parent, which is usually no passages at all, and that is why the parent codes in the picture show zero. With it on, the parent also shows everything from its children, which is what you want when you need a total for a theme. Turn it off again before you run queries after the break, because otherwise a single passage gets counted twice, once for the child and once for the parent.

Day two · Demonstration 9 of 17

Writing a memo: why a code exists, what you rejected, and what would change your mind

You made a code this afternoon that you were unsure about. Why did you make it?

The memo behind one code in the demonstration project, written on the day the code was made
The clicks, in order
  1. Under Coding, click Codes. Hold Control, click the code the memo is about, choose Memo Link, then Link to New Memo... The memo is then attached to that code.
  2. A Memo Properties window opens with the name selected. Give it a name that says what it is about, and not Untitled. Click Done, then type into the memo tab that has opened. It behaves like an ordinary text document.
  3. Write the date first, then what you decided, then what would change your mind.
  4. To open it again later, hold Control, click the code, choose Memo Link, then Open Linked Memo. All memos also sit under Notes on the left.
What you should see

Three parts go in a memo. Why the code exists, which is the decision. What else you considered and rejected, which is the alternative. And what would make you change it, which is the test. The memo on the screen has all three, and its third paragraph says that if no second study reports the same timing, the code belongs in the write up as one study’s finding and not as a theme.

Why this matters
Your codes and passages can be reconstructed by anybody with your project file, and your reasons cannot, so write the memo on the day you make the decision.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Memos. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/notes/memos.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Think back over the last hour. You made a code you were not sure about, and so did most of the room. The question on the slide is simply why you made it, and my real question is whether you will still know the answer in April. I did not know the answer for some of my own July labels by August, so we write it down, and the place NVivo gives you for that is a memo (Lumivero, n.d.).

The clicks are short. Under Coding, click Codes, hold Control and click the code the memo is about, choose Memo Link and then Link to New Memo, so that the memo is attached to that code and you can find it from the code later. A Memo Properties window opens with the name already selected, so type a name that says what the memo is about rather than leaving it as Untitled, because you will end up with a dozen, click Done, and then type into the memo tab that opens, since it behaves like an ordinary text document. Write the date first, then what you decided, then what would change your mind. To open it again later, hold Control, click the code, choose Memo Link and then Open Linked Memo, and all your memos also sit under Notes on the left.

What goes in it is three parts: why the code exists, what else you considered and rejected, and what would make you change your mind. Read the memo in the picture with me, because it is the real memo from the demonstration project and it has all three. The first paragraph says that the review’s frame has a code for aid effectiveness and one for remittance flows, and that neither of them holds what Le Dé and colleagues report, because their claim is about timing, and that is the why. The second paragraph says I could have folded it into aid effectiveness and chose not to, because that would bury a claim about timing inside a code about whether projects worked, and that is the alternative. The third says that two passages are coded here, both from one study, and that if no second study reports the same timing, this belongs in the write up as one study’s finding and not as a theme, and that is the test.

That third sentence is the one I would like you to copy. Writing down what would make you abandon your own code is the most useful sentence in a memo, because it stops you defending a theme you no longer believe in simply because you have already named it. Write one memo now, about a decision you made this afternoon, and take two minutes over it.

Day two · End of the first half

Save, make a second copy, and check that you have the four parts the classwork needs

If your laptop stopped working on the way home tonight, what would you have lost?

Saving

One file, and a copy of it somewhere else

Press Command and S on a Mac, or Control and S on Windows, and the title bar stops saying Edited and says Saved. Then close NVivo, find the file, and copy it to a drive or to cloud storage. Do that at the end of every session you work in it, including this one, before you leave the room.

What you should have by now

Check all four before the break

  1. Your paper imported, and its text selects.
  2. At least eight codes, each with a sentence in its description, and about twenty by the end of the afternoon.
  3. Your codes arranged in two levels, with parents and children.
  4. At least one passage coded to two codes at once, because the coding query after the break needs it.
Why this matters
If no passage in your paper has ever been coded twice, the coding query runs perfectly and returns nothing, and you cannot then tell whether you have made a mistake or found an absence.

Before the break, the question on the slide: if your laptop stopped working on the way home tonight, what would you have lost? For most of you the answer is this afternoon, and that is a bad answer, so save. Command and S on a Mac, Control and S on Windows, and watch the top of the window, where it stops saying Edited and says Saved.

Then do the part that people nod at and skip. Close NVivo, go and find the file, and copy it somewhere else, to a drive or to cloud storage, and do it now, before the break, because I want you to have done it once with me watching.

Now check four points, and I am going to walk round while you do. One, your paper is imported and its text selects. Two, you have at least eight codes, each with a sentence in its description, and go and look, because I know some of you skipped the descriptions; by five o’clock you will have about twenty. Three, your codes are in two levels, with parents and children. Four, and this is the one people miss, at least one passage in your paper is coded to two codes at once.

The fourth matters because it will cost you the classwork if you get it wrong. After the break we run a query that asks for every passage coded to two codes together, and if nothing in your paper has ever been coded twice, that query runs perfectly and returns nothing at all, so you will be sitting at home unable to tell whether you have made a mistake or found a real absence. If you have not got one, find a sentence that does two jobs and code it twice. Ten minutes, and we start again at three.

Day two · 16 October 2026 · Second half

Turning coded text into answers

Four queries, three charts, one codebook, and a plain account of what each of them cannot do

Everything in this half runs twiceFirst on the demonstration project, which holds four studies from the review with 44 coded passages, so that you can watch, and then on your own paper, so that you can do it. Two of the results go into your classwork.
The four queries

Two count words, and two count your coding

Word frequency counts the words in your material. Text search finds every place a word appears and shows what sits around it. The coding query finds passages coded to two codes at once. The crosstab counts your coded passages against something you know about each source, such as the region a study is about.

The three charts

Each one shows something, and hides something

The word cloud shows which words are frequent and nothing about what they mean. The word tree shows the words on either side of a term, which is how you see that one word is doing several jobs. The hierarchy chart shows which of your codes hold the most coded text.

Sources

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

This half is where coded text turns into something you can put in a sentence in a chapter. From here I close the empty project I built beside you and open the demonstration project, the file the pictures have shown all afternoon, because a query needs coded text to work on and four coded studies give it something to find. Everything runs twice: I run it on the demonstration project, which holds four studies from the review and the coding I did on them, and then you run the same query on your own paper. Two of these results go straight into your classwork.

There are four queries and they divide in two. Two of them count words, and they do not care whether you have coded anything at all. Two of them count your coding, and they are worth nothing if your coding is careless. Remember that division, because students often run the word queries, get an impressive looking picture, and think they have done an analysis, when they have counted words.

Every query this afternoon ends the same way. You run it, you look at what came back, and then you write one sentence that a reader could disagree with, and if you cannot write that sentence, the query has not told you anything yet.

Day two · Demonstration 10 of 17

The word frequency query counts the words in your material

Before I run it: which word do you think comes first in four studies about aid and remittances?

The result on the four studies, with the Similar Words column showing what was counted together
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Word Frequency.
  2. Leave Search in on Files and Externals to search everything, or choose Selected Items to search one paper.
  3. Under Finding matches, choose Include stemmed words. This counts remit, remits, remitted and remittances as one word instead of four.
  4. At Display words, choose 50 most frequent rather than All, and click Run Query.
  5. Read the Similar Words column on the right, which tells you exactly which words were counted together. If a grouping is wrong, that column is where you find out.
What you should see
remittances492project255
households252effects231
pacific205aid192
wiley150https137

What this cannot tell you. What any of these words means in context, or whether a paper argues for something or against it.

Why this matters
Wiley is the publisher and https starts every web address in the reference lists. Read the list and add words like these to the stop words list, under File then Project Properties, before you report anything.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Word frequency query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/word-frequency-query.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Guess before I run it. Four studies about aid and remittances, so which word comes first? Everyone is saying remittances, and everyone is right, and I want you to notice how little that tells us, because of course the word remittances is the most common word in four papers about remittances. If your word frequency query surprises you on the first line, look at your settings before you look at your data.

Explore, then Word Frequency, and there are three settings before you run it (Lumivero, n.d.). Leave Search in on Files and Externals to search everything; Selected Items would search one paper, and on your own project the two come to the same, because you have one file. Under Finding matches, choose Include stemmed words, which counts remit, remits, remitted and remittances as one thing instead of four, because without it your list is the same word four times. At Display words choose 50 most frequent, because no one reads a thousand. Now Run Query, and read the result with me: remittances 492, project 255, households 252, effects 231, pacific 205, aid 192.

Now look further down, at wiley with 150 and https with 137, and somebody tell me what those are. Wiley is the publisher, and https is the start of every web address in the reference lists, and neither has anything to do with aid or remittances. This is what a word count over real PDFs looks like, and if you put a word cloud in your dissertation with the publisher’s name in large letters, your examiner will know in one second that you never looked at your own output. You can deal with those: go to File, then Project Properties, where there is a stop words list, which is the list of words the query ignores, add wiley and https to it, and run the query again.

One column I would like you to use, on the far right, is called Similar Words. It tells you exactly which words were counted together when you turned on stemming, so if something looks strange in your own list, that column is where you find out why. Run it on your own paper now, with stemming on and fifty words, and tell me the first word that is not obviously about your topic.

Day two · Demonstration 11 of 17

The word cloud is the same counts drawn as sizes, and it carries less than the table it came from

Looking at this cloud, can you tell whether the studies say that aid works or that it does not?

The same 50 words as the table, drawn at sizes proportional to how often they occur
The clicks, in order
  1. Run the word frequency query as on the last slide.
  2. Above the results, click the Word Cloud tab. It takes a few seconds to draw.
  3. Click Gallery to change the colours if the default is hard to read.
  4. To put it in a document, hold Control, click the cloud, and choose Export.
  5. Then write the caption. The caption says what was counted, over what, and with which settings, or the picture means nothing.
What you should see

A caption that would pass. Word frequency across four studies, stemmed words grouped, 50 most frequent shown, publisher and web address terms not removed. The word remittances occurs 492 times and every other word occurs fewer than 260 times.

What this cannot tell you. What a word means in its sentence, whether an author agreed or disagreed with it, or which passages sit behind it.

Why this matters
A word cloud is usually the first thing a student puts in a findings chapter and among the weakest evidence of the afternoon, so use it to decide where to look next, and if you do put one in your dissertation, put the table next to it.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Word frequency query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/word-frequency-query.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Click the Word Cloud tab above your results, and it takes a few seconds to draw (Lumivero, n.d.). If the colours are hard to read, click Gallery and choose another set, and to put the cloud in a document, hold Control, click it, and choose Export. Now the question, and take a moment before you answer: looking at this cloud, can you tell whether these four studies say that aid works, or that it does not? Look properly, because the word aid is there, reasonably large.

You cannot, because nothing in this picture separates a paper arguing that aid projects succeed from one arguing that they fail, since the word aid appears the same number of times either way. That is what you need to understand about word clouds before you use one.

You will see word clouds in dissertations, and you will be tempted, because it is the one output from this software that looks like a finding, and it is among the weakest evidence we produce all afternoon. It shows you which words are frequent, and it cannot show what a word means, whether an author agreed with it, or which passages are behind it. So use it for one purpose: to decide where to look next. If a word you did not expect is large, that is worth chasing with the next query, and then you go and read the passages.

If you do put one in your dissertation, do two more steps. Put the table next to it, because the table has the counts, and write a caption that says what was counted, over what, and with which settings. There is one on the slide you can copy the shape of, and notice that it admits the publisher terms were not removed, which is the kind of admission that makes a reader trust the rest of your chapter.

Day two · Demonstration 12 of 17

The text search query finds every place a word appears, and the word tree shows what sits around it

The word support appears 152 times in these four studies. Is it always talking about the same thing?

The word tree for support: what comes immediately before and after the word each time it appears
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Text Search.
  2. Type the word or phrase in Search for. Put a phrase in quotation marks to search for the whole phrase.
  3. Choose Include stemmed words if you want supports and supported as well as support, and click Run Query.
  4. The Summary tab tells you which files the word is in and how many times. The Word Tree tab puts the searched word in the middle and the words around it branch out on either side.
  5. To turn the results into a code, click Save Results... and choose Codes, then open that code and read it, because it will be wrong in places.
What you should see
Quashie (2019), older adults in Havana and Bridgetown111
Le Dé and colleagues (2015), rural Samoa34
Brown and Leeves (2011), Fiji and Tonga5
Wood, Otor and Dornan (2022), Pacific aid projects2

What this cannot tell you. A passage that says the same thing in other words. A study about families helping each other that never uses the word support is invisible to this query, however relevant it is.

Why this matters
The branches into support include intergenerational, transnational, material, financial and health: five meanings under one word. Use the search to find passages worth reading, then code them yourself.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Text search query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/text-search-query.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Brown, R. P. C., & Leeves, G. (2011). Comparative effects of migrants’ remittances on composition of recipient household income in two small, island economies. Applied Economics, 43(27), 3965–3976. https://doi.org/10.1080/00036841003742611

Wood, T., Otor, S., & Dornan, M. (2022). Why are aid projects less effective in the Pacific? Development Policy Review, 40(3), e12573. https://doi.org/10.1111/dpr.12573

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The word support appears 152 times in these four studies, and the question is whether it is always talking about the same thing. Hold your answer. Explore, then Text Search, type support in the box, and if you ever want a whole phrase, put it in quotation marks, otherwise the query looks for the words separately. Choose Include stemmed words so that we also get supports and supported, and Run Query (Lumivero, n.d.).

Look at the Summary tab first. 111 of those occurrences are in one study, the one by Quashie about older adults in Havana and Bridgetown, 34 are in the Samoa study, 5 in the Fiji and Tonga study and 2 in the Pacific aid projects study. That distribution is itself worth knowing, because the paper about older people talks about support constantly since that is what it is about, and you would want to know that before you started counting across all four.

Now click the Word Tree tab, which is the picture on the slide. The word support sits in the middle, and everything that comes immediately before and after it in each of those 152 occurrences branches out on either side. Read the branches with me: intergenerational support, transnational support, material support, financial support, health support. That is five different meanings under one word, and a count of 152 hides every one of them.

So the answer to my question is no, it is not always the same thing, and no query that counts strings of letters can tell you that. A code is attached to a meaning that you judged, and a search is attached to a string of letters, which is the whole difference between coding and searching, and it is why the coding you did before the break is worth more than anything on this slide.

There is a button called Save Results, which turns your search into a code. It is useful for finding passages quickly, and if you use it, you must then open that code and read what it put there, because it will have picked up sentences that use the word in a sense you did not want.

Day two · Demonstration 13 of 17

The coding query finds passages you coded to two codes at once

Which two of your own codes would be interesting to find together in one passage?

The query with Coded to set to all of these codes and two codes chosen, and its result: one passage, from one study
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Queries, then Coding...
  2. On the row that says Coded to, leave the menu on all of these codes. This is the difference between asking for both and asking for either.
  3. On the same row, click the small round button at the right. A list of your codes opens.
  4. Expand a parent to reach its children, tick the two codes you want, and click Select.
  5. Click Run Query and read the Reference tab. Each result names the file it came from and gives you the passage.
What you should see

Asking for Aid effectiveness, delivery and critique together with Remittance flows, motives and behaviour returns one passage, from Le Dé and colleagues (2015, p. 653): remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher.

What this cannot tell you. Whether one passage is enough. One result is a lead and not a finding, and the next step is to look for the same pattern in other sources.

Why this matters
The query found that sentence in about thirty seconds, and only because one passage had been coded twice, by hand, before the break; this is also the query the classwork asks you to run.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Coding query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/coding-query.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

This is the second query your classwork asks for, so follow closely. The question first: look at your own list of codes, and tell me which two of them would be interesting to find together in one passage. Not two that obviously go together, because then you learn nothing, but two that you would not expect to meet, and write them down.

Explore, then Queries, then Coding, and look at the row that says Coded to and at the small menu that says all of these codes (Lumivero, n.d.). That menu is the whole query. All of these codes means both must be present, while any of these codes means either will do, which merges your two codes together and is almost never what you meant, so leave it on all. Click the small round button at the right of that row, and your codes appear; expand a parent to get at its children, tick the two you want, click Select, and Run Query.

Watch what comes back on my screen. One passage, from the Samoa study, and I am reading it exactly as it is coded: remittances interact with external aid since remittances increase when external aid is low and decrease when external aid is higher (Le Dé et al., 2015, p. 653). Now think about what just happened. The question behind that whole review is whether aid and remittances work on each other, I asked four studies for any passage that was about aid effectiveness and about remittance behaviour at the same time, and this sentence came back in about thirty seconds.

That query could only find it because I had coded that one sentence twice, by hand, before the break. If I had coded it only to remittances, this query would return nothing and I would never see it. The software found nothing that I had not already put there; what it did was find something I had put there and forgotten, which is a smaller claim than people usually make for it, and a true one.

One result is a lead and not a finding, and what I would do next is look for the same pattern in more studies. Run your own query now, and if it comes back empty, that is because you have no passage coded twice, so go and make one.

Day two · Demonstration 14 of 17 · Watch this one, because it needs more than one source

Giving each source its facts: a classification sheet makes a source a case with attributes

You have coded a theme. How would you find out whether it appears more in one kind of source than another?

The classification sheet: four studies, each with four facts recorded about it
The clicks, in order
  1. Make a spreadsheet: the first column is the name of each source exactly as it appears in NVivo, every other column is one fact about it. Save it as a .csv file.
  2. On the ribbon click Import, then Classifications, then Classification Sheet... and choose your file.
  3. At step 2, change Classification type to Case Classification, and under Create new classification type a name for what these cases are. Here it is Study; for interviews it might be Participant.
  4. Click through steps 3 and 4 and then Import. Your cases appear under Cases on the left.
  5. Attach each case to its source: select the file under Files, on the Home tab click Code, then Code Files, then To Existing Codes or Cases..., click Cases, tick the matching case and click Select.
What you should see

Four studies are four cases, each with four facts: the region it is about, the flow it studies, the kind of evidence it uses, and the year. Your classwork paper is one source, so you watch this one rather than repeating it.

What this cannot tell you. Anything about a fact you did not record. If you never wrote down which region a study is about, no query can compare regions.

Why this matters
With cases in place you can ask whether the women you interviewed describe an obligation differently from the men. Record these facts while you collect your data.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). About classifications. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 21, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/classifications/about-classifications.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The next two demonstrations are ones you watch rather than repeat, because they need more than one source, and your classwork paper is one source. I am showing them because your dissertation will have twelve interviews or four focus groups, and this is the step that decides whether that project can answer a comparative question. The question: you have coded a theme, so how would you find out whether it appears more in one kind of source than another, more in the Pacific studies than the Caribbean one, or more in the interviews with women than with men?

At the moment you could not, because NVivo knows nothing about your sources except their file names, so we tell it. A case is a source with facts attached to it. In my project the four studies are four cases, and each one has four facts recorded about it, which region it is about, which flow it studies, what kind of evidence it uses, and the year, and you can see them in the picture (Lumivero, n.d.).

You could type all that in by hand, and I would rather you did not. Make a spreadsheet instead, with the name of each source in the first column, exactly as it appears in NVivo, and one fact in every other column, and save it as a csv file. Then Import, Classifications, Classification Sheet. A point to watch at step 2: it opens on File Classification and you want Case Classification, so change it, then type a name for what these cases are; mine are studies so I called it Study, and if yours are interviews, call it Participant. Click through and import, and your cases appear under Cases on the left.

Now the step that people forget, and if you forget it nothing works. Creating the cases records the facts, and it does not connect them to anything, so you have to attach each case to its source: select the file under Files, on the Home tab click Code, then Code Files, then To Existing Codes or Cases, click Cases on the left of that window, tick the case that matches, and click Select, for every source.

For your dissertation, record these facts while you are collecting your data and not afterwards, because what you know about a participant on the day you interview them is easy to write down, and reconstructing it from a transcript in April is not.

Day two · Demonstration 15 of 17 · Watch this one, because it needs more than one source

The crosstab query counts your coded passages against a fact about each source

Three of these studies are about the Pacific and one is about the Caribbean. What can you safely say from that?

Every code against the region the study is about, shown as coding references, with darker green for larger counts
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Queries, then Crosstab... Close the help panel that opens the first time.
  2. Under Codes, click + and tick the codes you want down the rows. Ticking the top box takes all of them, which is what the screen shows.
  3. Under Show code against, leave Attributes chosen. Set Classification to the kind of case you made, here Study, and Attributes to the fact you want across the columns, here Region.
  4. Click Run Query.
  5. Click the Results tab. Under Show results as choose Coding references to count passages, and choose a Heat map.
What you should see
Pacific studies3Caribbean studies1
Aid effectiveness3 and 0Gender and social relations0 and 2
Health and education1 and 2All passages36 and 8

What this cannot tell you. Whether the Pacific talks about aid effectiveness more than the Caribbean, because three studies sit behind the first column and one behind the second.

Why this matters
When I first ran this query the Church, Gender and Food rows were empty, and the text was not: Le Dé and colleagues (2015, pp. 664 to 665) give church donations 12% of remittances and food 13%. An empty row is a question you take back to the paper, not a finding about absence.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Crosstab query. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/queries/crosstab-query.htm

Le Dé, L., Gaillard, J. C., Friesen, W., & Smith, F. M. (2015). Remittances in the face of disasters: A case study of rural Samoa. Environment, Development and Sustainability, 17(3), 653–672. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10668-014-9559-0

Quashie, N. T. (2019). Social welfare and remittances to older adults in two Caribbean cities. International Migration, 57(5), 71–88. https://doi.org/10.1111/imig.12591

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

This is the query that compares, and it only works because of the cases we made on the last slide, so again you watch this one on the demonstration project. Explore, then Queries, then Crosstab, and a help panel opens the first time you use it, which is worth reading once, then Close (Lumivero, n.d.). Under Codes click the plus and tick what you want down the rows; I have ticked the top box, which takes every code. Classification is Study, which is the kind of case I made, and Attributes is Region, which is the fact I want across the top. Run Query.

Then click the Results tab on the right. NVivo shows cases coded by default, which counts how many studies mention each code, and I am changing it to Coding references, which counts the passages, and choosing a green heat map, because a grid of small numbers is hard to read and the shading makes the pattern visible. The two columns now add up to 36 and 8, which is all 44 coded passages in the project.

Now the question from the top of the slide, and I would like a careful answer. Three of these studies are about the Pacific and one is about the Caribbean, and aid effectiveness has three passages in the Pacific column and no passages in the Caribbean column. What can you safely say? Very little, because you have three Pacific studies and one Caribbean study, so of course the Pacific column is fuller, and a bigger number in a column with three studies behind it and a smaller number in a column with one study behind it tells you about your sample and not about the world. Write that sentence down, because it is a common mistake with this table, and an examiner will look for it.

Now look at three rows that were empty when I first ran this query: Church, religion and spirituality, Gender and social relations, and Food security and food systems. Every cell in those three rows was zero, and I was tempted to write that four studies about money moving between family members never discuss church giving, gender or food. That would have been wrong. I went back to the text. On page 664 of the Samoa study the authors say that about 12% of remittances went to church donations before the tsunami, and on page 665 that 13% went to food, and Quashie reports that children in Bridgetown were less likely to send to fathers than to mothers (Le Dé et al., 2015, pp. 664 to 665; Quashie, 2019, p. 81). Those rows were empty because I had not coded those passages, not because the studies were silent, and the table on the screen now shows two passages in each of them. So an empty row is a question you take back to the paper, and only after you have reread the paper may it become a sentence about absence. That is phase four again, and it is the most useful work this table did for me.

Day two · Demonstration 16 of 17

The hierarchy chart draws each code at a size proportional to how much text sits under it

Which of your codes do you think holds the most text, and are you about to be wrong?

The treemap: each parent is a block, its children sit inside it, and the area follows the number of passages
The clicks, in order
  1. On the ribbon click Explore, then Hierarchy Chart.
  2. Under Visualize, leave Coding for Codes chosen.
  3. Under Size by, choose Coding references to size by the number of passages, or Items coded to size by how many sources each code appears in. Look at both.
  4. Switch between Treemap and Sunburst at the top. Rest the pointer on any block to see the code name and its counts.
  5. To use it in a document, hold Control, click the chart, and choose Export.
What you should see

On my screen the largest block is Livelihoods and wellbeing, and inside it the largest child is Livelihood strategies and household economy, with five passages. Rest the pointer on any block and a box gives its counts; on my project Health and education shows three coding references from two sources.

What this cannot tell you. Whether a big block is a theme that matters or a code that has become the place where everything else goes. Only opening the code and reading it tells you which.

Why this matters
A big block means you coded a lot of text to that code, not that the theme is important, so open it and read it before you report it, and say in the caption that the chart is a check on your coding.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Hierarchy charts. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/vizualizations/hierarchy-charts.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

Guess before I show you. Which of your codes holds the most text? Write it down, and now run it and see whether you were right. Explore, then Hierarchy Chart, and leave Coding for Codes chosen (Lumivero, n.d.). You get a treemap, which is your whole set of codes drawn as blocks, with each parent as a block and its children inside it, and the area of each block following the number of passages under it. On my screen the largest block is Livelihoods and wellbeing, and inside it the largest child is Livelihood strategies and household economy, with five passages.

Switch to the Sunburst tab, which gives the same information as rings, with parents in the middle and children on the outside. Some people read one more easily than the other, and there is no right answer, so use whichever you can read. Rest the pointer on any block and a box tells you the code and its counts, and on my project Health and education shows three coding references from two sources.

One setting worth trying, under Size by. Coding references sizes the blocks by how many passages are under each code, and Items coded sizes them by how many different sources the code appears in, and those are two different questions. A code with fifteen passages that are all from one interview is a very different result from a code with eight passages spread across eight interviews, and switching between those two settings shows you the difference in about two seconds.

Now the same warning as for the word cloud. A big block means you coded a lot of text to that code, and it does not mean the theme is important. Often a block that is much bigger than everything around it is a code that has turned into the Culture code we talked about on the first day, the one that holds everything, so when you see one, do not put it in your dissertation, open it and read it. Used that way the chart is a check on your own coding, and if you export it for a document, hold Control, click it, choose Export, and write a caption that says what the size represents.

Day two · Demonstration 17 of 17

Exporting the codebook: your codes, your definitions and your counts in one document

If you exported yours right now, how many of the description boxes would be empty?

The lower half of the demonstration project’s codebook, exported on 23 September 2026 and opened as a document: name, description, sources and references for each code
The clicks, in order
  1. On the left, under Coding, click Codes.
  2. On the ribbon click Share, then Export, then Export Codebook...
  3. Leave the tick on Codes to take all of them, and click Select.
  4. In Save As name the file, choose where it goes, leave File Format on MS Word (.docx), and click OK.
  5. Open it and read the description column. Every empty cell is a code you cannot defend, and you can still fix it today.
What you should see

Sources is how many different files the code appears in, and References is how many separate passages are coded to it. Growth and macroeconomy, 3 sources and 3 passages, runs across the literature. Livelihood strategies and household economy, 2 sources and 5 passages, is two studies talking repeatedly. Remittances arrive before the aid does, 1 source and 2 passages, is one study said twice, which is a lead and not a theme, exactly as the memo says.

Why this matters
This one document is what a supervisor or an examiner asks for first, and your classwork has to include it.
Sources

Lumivero. (n.d.). Export codes and codebook. NVivo 15 for Mac help. Retrieved September 22, 2026, from https://help-nv.qsrinternational.com/15/mac/Content/nodes/export-nodes.htm

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The question first, and answer it to yourself: if you exported your codebook this minute, how many of the description boxes would be empty? That is why we are doing this now and not at home.

Under Coding on the left, click Codes. On the ribbon, Share, then Export, then Export Codebook, leave the tick on Codes, which takes all of them, and click Select. In the Save As window, name the file, leave the format on Word, and click OK (Lumivero, n.d.). Now open it. It is a table with four columns, and the picture shows the lower half of the demonstration project’s table: the code name, the description, the number of sources it appears in, and the number of passages coded to it.

Look at my numbers, because three of them tell a story. Growth and macroeconomy has three sources and three passages, which means three of the four studies mention it once each, so it is a topic that runs across the literature. Livelihood strategies and household economy has two sources and five passages, so two studies talk about it repeatedly, and it is concentrated. And Remittances arrive before the aid does has one source and two passages, which is one study, said twice, and that is not a theme yet, it is a lead, exactly as the memo says.

That distinction between sources and passages is worth holding on to. A code with twelve passages all from one interview is one person talking, and a code with four passages from four different people is a pattern. The exported table is where you see the difference. Notice also Food security, one source and two passages, and Church and Gender, higher up the table, are the same. When I first ran the crosstab those three rows said zero and zero, and it was this table that sent me back to the Samoa study and to Quashie to code what I had missed.

Now look at your own description column, because every empty cell is a code you cannot defend. You have about twenty minutes before we finish, and filling them in now, while you still remember what you meant, takes a minute each. Export it, look at it, fix it, and export it again, because the second export is the one you attach to your classwork.

Day two · Where the software stops

NVivo stores, retrieves and counts what you coded, and every judgement in the analysis stays yours

Of everything we did this afternoon, which step did the software decide?

It did this

Kept the record and did the counting

It held four studies, 23 codes and 44 coded passages, found the one passage coded to two codes in about thirty seconds, and counted the coding against a fact about each source. Every one of those tasks is slow and error prone on paper.

It did not do this

Decide what any passage means

It did not choose a single passage, write a single code name, or judge that two labels were saying the same thing. The coding query found that sentence only because a person had coded it twice, so the software surfaced a judgement that had already been made.

And it cannot do this

Rescue coding that was done carelessly

Every query this afternoon ran on your codes. A word count works on any material at all, and on its own it says little. Everything worth having came out of coding that somebody did by hand, so the quality of the output is fixed before you open the Explore menu.

The sentence to write in your methods chapterNVivo was used to manage the coding, to retrieve coded passages, and to produce the counts reported. Not that it was used to analyse the data, and not that themes emerged from it. Wiltshier (2011) sets out what the software does and does not do for the analysis, in a short open access paper.
One phrase to stop usingThe phrase themes emerged gives to a process the work that a person did, and Braun and Clarke (2019) object to it directly. Writing that you identified the themes, and naming how, is more accurate and easier to defend, because a reader can then ask you about the decision.
Sources

Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2019). Reflecting on reflexive thematic analysis. Qualitative Research in Sport, Exercise and Health, 11(4), 589–597. https://doi.org/10.1080/2159676X.2019.1628806

Wiltshier, F. (2011). Researching with NVivo. Forum: Qualitative Social Research, 12(1). https://doi.org/10.17169/fqs-12.1.1628

de Waegh, R. (2026). ISS5220 demonstration project [NVivo 15 project with four studies, codebook exported 22 September 2026]. Islands and Small States Institute, University of Malta.

The question on the slide: of everything we did this afternoon, which step did the software decide? Think about it properly and name one.

Not one of them. It did not choose a single passage, it did not write a single code name, and it did not decide that two of your labels were saying the same thing. When the coding query found that sentence about remittances and aid, it found it because a person had coded that sentence twice, by hand, an hour earlier, so the software surfaced a judgement that had already been made. That is real and useful work, and it is a much smaller claim than the one people usually make.

What it did do is worth having. It held four studies, 23 codes and 44 coded passages, and it retrieved and counted them without losing any, which on paper is slow, and I would have made mistakes. So here is the sentence to write in your methods chapter, and I would like you to write it down now: NVivo was used to manage the coding, to retrieve coded passages, and to produce the counts reported. Not that NVivo was used to analyse the data, because it was not; you were.

And one phrase I would like you to stop using: themes emerged from the data. They did not emerge. You identified them, on the second day, having made a series of decisions you could have made differently, and Braun and Clarke (2019) object to the phrase for exactly that reason. Writing that you identified the themes is more accurate and it is easier to defend, because your examiner can then ask you about your decision instead of asking you about a process that no one was in charge of. Wiltshier (2011) has a short open access paper on what this software does and does not do for the analysis, and it is linked in the sources, so read it before you write your methods chapter rather than after.

Day two · What you hand in by 27 October

Every part of the classwork was produced on a screen you have already used this afternoon

Which of the five parts are you not able to produce right now, at this desk?

What to hand in

400 to 500 words, with your codebook and your screenshots attached

  1. What the paper is about and why it interests you.
  2. The codes you made and how you arranged them, with the codebook attached.
  3. How you set up the word frequency query and what it returned, with a screenshot.
  4. How you set up the coding query for two of your codes together and what it returned, with a screenshot.
  5. Two sentences on what the queries did not tell you.
Where each part came from this afternoon

Nothing here is new

  1. Your own reading of the paper, before you coded it.
  2. The codebook export we just did, with the description column filled in.
  3. The word frequency query, stemmed words on, 50 words, with the junk words noted.
  4. The coding query, on all of these codes, which needs a passage coded twice.
  5. The line that starts What this cannot tell you, which has been on the query slides all afternoon.
Why this matters
Part five takes the least time and is where marks are most often lost, by writing nothing: name the specific thing your specific query could not see in your specific paper.

The classwork is due on 27 October, and it is four hundred to five hundred words with two attachments. Read the left card with me and then answer the question on the slide: which of the five parts can you not produce right now, sitting at this desk?

For most of you the answer is not one of them, and that is deliberate. Part one is your own reading of the paper. Part two is the codebook you exported twenty minutes ago. Part three is the word frequency query we ran at the start of this half, and part four is the coding query, which needs a passage coded to two codes, which is why I asked you to check that before the break.

Part five is worth as much as the others, it takes the least time, and it is where people write nothing. You have heard the answer all afternoon, in the line that starts What this cannot tell you on the query slides. A word frequency query cannot tell you what a word meant in its sentence, and we saw that with the word support, which turned out to carry five different meanings. A coding query cannot tell you whether one passage is enough to claim anything.

Write those two down, and do not write that the method has limitations, which says nothing. Name the specific thing your specific query could not see in your specific paper, because that sentence is how I tell the difference between somebody who ran a query and somebody who understood it. Bring me the paper you are working on if you are unsure about it, and if your coding query came back empty, come and see me now rather than emailing me the night before the deadline.

Last slide. A theme can be defended when a reader can open your codebook, follow each code back to the passages under it, and see who decided what, and if your work does that, it does not matter whether you used this software or a notebook.

The method is six phases, and the fourth one, opening a theme and reading everything in it, is the one that catches your mistakes (Braun and Clarke, 2006). The software keeps the record and does the counting, and nothing in it decided anything this afternoon. Three habits are worth more than any button in the programme: write the definition when you make the code, write the memo on the day you make the decision, and open your own codes and read them.

One question to take home, and it is on the slide: which of your own codes would you not be able to defend tomorrow, and what would it take to fix that tonight? For most of you the answer is a sentence in a description box.

You have your project file, you have a codebook, and you have a classwork you can finish this week. The NVivo help pages for Mac and Windows are open to anyone and cover everything we did, the Beekhuyzen and Bazeley book is in the library, and my office is at the Islands and Small States Institute, so come and find me, because a question in October is much easier to answer than the same question in May.

Thank you for the two days. Save your project before you close your laptop, and copy it somewhere else before you leave the room.
